blocks.text: A single line of firmware, PORTB = 0x08, lights a lamp on pin 3, but it also forces the other seven pins on that port to zero, including the one holding a relay closed. Microcontroller peripherals are controlled by writing bits in registers, and every write must change only the bits you intend.

blocks.markdown: A **register** is a memory location, at a fixed address, connected to hardware. Writing it configures or drives a peripheral; reading it reports hardware state. A **GPIO (general-purpose input/output)** port has a *direction register* (one bit per pin: 1 = output, 0 = input), an *output register* (the level driven on output pins, or the pull-up enable for inputs on many devices) and an *input register* (the level read from the pins). Names vary by device; here we use DDRx, PORTx and PINx as typical examples.

blocks.title: Read-modify-write with bit masks
blocks.text: To change one bit without disturbing the others, combine the register with a mask built by shifting: $(1<<n)$ is a value with only bit $n$ set. Set: `REG |= (1<<n)`. Clear: `REG &= ~(1<<n)`. Toggle: `REG ^= (1<<n)`. Test: `REG & (1<<n)`.

blocks.title: Configuring pins
blocks.prompt: A port has DDRB = 0x21 (pins 5 and 0 are outputs) and PORTB = 0x00. Make pin 3 an output, make pin 0 an input with its internal pull-up enabled, and leave everything else unchanged. Give the final register values.

steps.text: Set bit 3 of DDRB to make pin 3 an output: `DDRB |= (1<<3);`
Clear bit 0 of DDRB to make pin 0 an input: `DDRB &= ~(1<<0);`. The mask $\sim(1<<0)$ is 0xFE.
Writing a 1 to the PORTB bit of an input enables its pull-up on this type of device: `PORTB |= (1<<0);`
Check: the other bits of DDRB (bit 5 stays an output) were not disturbed.

blocks.answer: DDRB = 0x28 (bits 5 and 3 outputs, others inputs) and PORTB = 0x1 (pull-up on pin 0).

blocks.markdown: **Timers and PWM.** A hardware timer counts clock pulses. A **prescaler** divides the clock by $(PSC+1)$, and the counter counts from 0 up to the auto-reload value $ARR$ and restarts, so the period is $(ARR+1)$ timer ticks. A compare value $CCR$ switches the output high while the counter is below it, which gives the duty cycle.

blocks.caption: PWM frequency and duty cycle for an edge-aligned timer (counts are integers)

blocks.title: Computing prescaler and period
blocks.prompt: A 72 MHz timer with a 16-bit counter (ARR at most 65 535) must generate 1 kHz PWM at 30 percent duty. Choose PSC, ARR and CCR.

steps.text: 72 000 does not fit in 16 bits, so a prescaler is needed. Choose $PSC+1=2$ (PSC = 1).

blocks.answer: PSC = 1, ARR = 35999, CCR = 10800 gives 1 kHz at 30 percent duty.

blocks.markdown: **Why `volatile`?** A compiler assumes that a variable changes only when your code changes it. It may therefore keep the value in a CPU register, or even delete a loop that seems to wait for something nothing in the code can change. A variable modified by an **interrupt service routine** or a **hardware register** can change at any time, so it must be declared `volatile`, which forces the compiler to read or write memory on every access.

items: `volatile uint8_t flag;` for a flag set by an ISR and tested in `while(!flag);`.
`volatile uint32_t * const STATUS = (uint32_t *)0x40010000;` for a memory-mapped status register.
`volatile` does not make a multi-byte access atomic: a 16-bit value on an 8-bit CPU can still change between the two byte reads.

blocks.title: Do not assign a whole register to change one pin
blocks.text: Writing `PORTB = 0x08;` sets pin 3 but also clears every other pin of that port. Use the bit operations above unless you deliberately mean to set the whole register.

blocks.title: Datasheet is the contract
blocks.text: Register names, bit positions and prescaler formulas differ between devices (some timers count $ARR$ or $ARR+1$ ticks, some have fixed divide-by-N values). Always check the device datasheet before computing values.

points: GPIO direction, output and input registers are manipulated with bit masks: `|=` to set, `&= ~` to clear, `^=` to toggle.
PWM frequency is $f_{clk}/((PSC+1)(ARR+1))$ and duty is $CCR/(ARR+1)$.
If $f_{clk}/f_{PWM}$ exceeds the counter range, use a prescaler.
`volatile` stops the compiler caching or removing accesses to variables changed by hardware or an ISR, but does not make multi-byte accesses atomic.

questions.stem: Which statement sets bit 4 of PORTB to 1 and leaves the other bits unchanged?

distractorRationale.b: This clears bit 4 instead of setting it.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: OR with a single-bit mask sets that bit only.

questions.explanation: OR-ing with a mask that has only bit 4 set forces that bit to 1 and leaves all others as they were. Plain assignment would overwrite the other bits with zero.

questions.stem: Which statement configures pin 2 of a port as an input (1 = output in the direction register) without changing other pins?

distractorRationale.a: This sets the bit and makes the pin an output.
distractorRationale.b: This makes pin 2 the only output and changes all others.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: AND with an inverted mask clears the bit.

questions.explanation: Clearing bit 2 of the direction register makes that pin an input. The mask $\sim(1<<2)$ has a 0 only in bit 2, so AND-ing leaves the rest unchanged.

questions.stem: A timer runs from a 16 MHz clock with PSC+1 = 8 and ARR+1 = 200. If the prescaler is changed to PSC+1 = 32 with ARR unchanged, what happens to the PWM frequency?

options.text: It falls by a factor of 4
It rises by a factor of 4
It falls by a factor of 32

questions.correctOptionText: It falls by a factor of 4

distractorRationale.a: Correct: frequency is inversely proportional to the prescaler.
distractorRationale.b: A larger divider slows the timer, so the frequency cannot rise.
distractorRationale.c: The prescaler enters the frequency formula.
distractorRationale.d: The ratio of the prescaler values is 4, not 32.

questions.explanation: The frequency is $f_{clk}/((PSC+1)(ARR+1))$, so multiplying the prescaler by 4 divides the frequency by 4, from 10 kHz to 2.5 kHz.

questions.stem: A firmware loop `while (!data_ready) { }` waits for `data_ready`, which is set by an ISR. What can go wrong if the variable is not declared volatile?

options.text: The variable will be stored in flash
The loop exits immediately in all cases
The compiler may keep the value in a register and the loop may never exit

questions.correctOptionText: The compiler may keep the value in a register and the loop may never exit

distractorRationale.a: Declaring volatile does not affect whether the ISR runs.
distractorRationale.b: Storage location is unrelated to volatile.
distractorRationale.c: The behaviour is optimisation-dependent, not an automatic immediate exit.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: caching in a register hides the ISR's update.

questions.explanation: Since nothing in the loop changes the variable, the optimiser may read it once and loop forever on the cached value. Declaring it `volatile` forces a memory read on every pass.

questions.stem: On an 8-bit microcontroller, a 16-bit counter variable is updated in an ISR and declared volatile. The main loop copies it with `x = count;`. What risk remains?

options.text: The compiler will remove the read
The ISR will be unable to modify the variable
The main loop may read one byte before and one byte after an ISR update and get an inconsistent value

questions.correctOptionText: The main loop may read one byte before and one byte after an ISR update and get an inconsistent value

distractorRationale.a: volatile makes the compiler keep the read, not remove it.
distractorRationale.b: volatile allows modification by an ISR.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: volatile does not guarantee atomicity.
distractorRationale.d: The sign is unrelated to the access order.

questions.explanation: volatile prevents caching but does not make the 2-byte read indivisible. If the ISR fires between the two byte reads, the copy mixes old and new bytes, so the read should be made with interrupts briefly disabled.

questions.stem: A timer has a 16 MHz clock, PSC+1 = 8 and ARR+1 = 100. Calculate the PWM frequency in kilohertz.
questions.explanation: The frequency is $16\times10^6/(8\times100)=20\,000$ Hz, which is 20 kHz. The period is 50 microseconds.

questions.stem: A 72 MHz timer with PSC = 71 produces a 1 MHz counter clock. For a 50 Hz servo signal (period 20 ms), find the value to load into ARR (the counter runs from 0 to ARR).
questions.explanation: The period is $1/50=20$ ms, which is 20 000 ticks at 1 MHz. Since the period is $ARR+1$ ticks, $ARR=19\,999$.

questions.stem: A 48 MHz timer with PSC = 0 must generate 25 kHz PWM at 37.5 percent duty. Find the CCR value (an integer count).

Describe how to configure pin 5 of a port as an output driven high and pin 1 as an input, without disturbing other pins. Explain read-modify-write, the masks used, and why a whole-register assignment is hazardous.
markingGuide: Sets the direction bit for the output: `DDR |= (1<<5)` (1 mark)
Clears the direction bit for the input: `DDR &= ~(1<<1)` (1 mark)
Drives the output high with `PORT |= (1<<5)` (1 mark)
Explains read-modify-write: read the register, change one bit with a mask, write back, so other bits keep their values (2 marks)
Explains `REG = value` overwrites all bits and can switch other pins or peripherals unintentionally (2 marks)
Mentions checking the datasheet for bit meanings (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Each operation uses a single-bit mask and a read-modify-write so only that pin changes; assignment would overwrite the other seven bits.

questions.stem: Explain what the `volatile` qualifier does and give two situations where it is required. Describe what the compiler might do without it, and name one problem that `volatile` does not solve.
markingGuide: States volatile forces a real memory access on every read or write and prevents caching or removal (2 marks)
Situation 1: a flag or buffer shared between an ISR and the main loop (1 mark)
Situation 2: a memory-mapped hardware register such as a status register (1 mark)
Explains that without it the compiler may hold the value in a CPU register, or delete a wait loop (2 marks)
States volatile does not give atomicity for multi-byte variables or ordering across threads, so critical sections are needed (2 marks)
questions.explanation: volatile tells the compiler the value can change outside its knowledge, so every access must reach memory. It does not make multi-byte accesses indivisible.
